notes.summary: CS 61A teaches programming as abstraction — managing complexity by hiding detail — using Python, Scheme, and SQL in one arc. The live Fall 2026 edition opens with the course's philosophy, the tools (Python 3, terminal, editor, ok autograder), and the first ideas: expressions, statements, and the read-eval loop. Everything is taught at the current course site, updated for this semester.
notes.focus: Complete lab 00 fully — environment setup done now pays off every week. Then write one expression and one statement and say out loud what each returns or does.

notes.summary: Functions are named abstractions: bind a name in the environment, define parameters, return a value. This lecture covers def statements, call expressions, the evaluation order (evaluate operator, then operands left to right, then apply), and pure vs non-pure functions like print. The environment model of names starts here and never stops growing.
notes.focus: Draw the environment diagram for a two-function program by hand. Getting diagrams right now makes recursion diagrams trivial later.

notes.summary: Conditional statements and iteration: if/elif/else, boolean logic with and/or/not (short-circuiting), while loops, and the debugging discipline of print and assert. The lecture frames control as the shape of a program's execution and emphasizes writing loop invariants you can state in one sentence.
notes.focus: Rewrite one while loop as a recursive function and back. Being bilingual between iteration and recursion is the core skill of the whole course.

notes.summary: The first big idea of 61A: functions are values. They can be passed as arguments, returned from other functions, and nested inside closures that remember their enclosing names. Higher-order functions (map-like apply_twice, currying, and the famous lambdas) let you abstract patterns of computation, not just data.
notes.focus: Write make_adder, then make_multiplier, then a general make_op without looking. Then write a one-line version of each with lambda.

notes.summary: Environments are the precise model of names: global frame, local frames, and the parent chain that closures follow. This lecture walks nested def statements and shows exactly where every name is looked up. If you can predict lookup order (current frame, then parents), recursion's environment diagrams become mechanical.
notes.focus: For a function defined inside a function, list every name it can see when called. Then run the code and verify with a drawn diagram.

notes.summary: Recursion solves a problem in terms of smaller copies of itself. The discipline: state the base case, state the recursive leap of faith, and never trace more than two levels. Environment diagrams for recursion show multiple frames of the same function — deep, but the rules are unchanged.
notes.focus: Implement is_prime recursively, then recursively reverse a string. If tempted to trace five levels, trace exactly two and trust the rest — that is the skill.

notes.summary: Tree recursion: a function that calls itself more than once. Fibonacci is the gateway, and counting the calls reveals exponential blowup — the motivation for memoization. This lecture also solves combinatorial counting problems (counting partitions) where tree recursion is the natural shape of the answer.
notes.focus: Write a recursive count_partitions, then hand-count the calls for small inputs. Add memoization and feel the speedup — the same trick will return in 61B and every algorithms course.

notes.summary: Sequences abstract ordered data: lists, tuples, ranges, strings, and 2D containers. The lecture covers slicing semantics (including negative indices), for over sequences, list comprehension, and the abstraction boundary — the same operations on any sequence type. The reading pairs with the containers lecture (12) for the full picture.
notes.focus: Predict slice results (x[1:4], x[::-1], x[::2]) before running. Then write one function that works on any sequence and say which operations needed the abstraction.

notes.summary: Object-oriented programming arrives as a natural extension of data abstraction: classes bundle state (attributes) and behavior (methods) behind a constructor. You meet __init__, self, bound methods, and the class/object distinction. The mutable-state trade-off — shared data versus pure functions — is the design question the course keeps returning to.
concepts: Attribute lookup on objects and classes
notes.focus: Implement a small class (Account) with deposit/withdraw guards. Then break it deliberately by aliasing two names to one object and observing shared mutation.

notes.summary: Trees are the quintessential recursive data structure: a root and a list of subtrees, described entirely by a constructor (tree, label) and selectors (label, branches). The lecture covers recursive processing of trees — counting leaves, depth, pruning — while respecting the abstraction barrier. These skills map directly onto CS 61B's tree structures next course.
notes.focus: Write a function that counts tree leaves, then one that builds a tree of squares of the original labels. Both should read like two-line poems.

notes.summary: Mutation week: mutable lists interacting with functions that hold state, nonlocal to rebind enclosing names, iterators as one-pass sequences, and generators that produce values lazily with yield. These tools — plus the mutation hazards that come with them — complete the Python core before the course pivots to Scheme and interpreters.
notes.focus: Write a generator that yields a running average. Then trigger the classic bug (mutating a list while looping) once on purpose to see it bite.

notes.summary: Checkpoint on the Python half: functions, environments, recursion, sequences, objects, and mutation. Work the current semester's review sheet and at least one past exam under time pressure. The second half of 61A — Scheme, SQL, and building an interpreter — assumes all of this is fluent.
notes.focus: Grade your own past exam against the solutions and write down the rule you missed for each wrong answer. The rule, not the answer, is what transfers.

lessons.title: Final: Scheme, Interpreters, and Programs as Data

notes.summary: The course finale is programs that read programs: you study a Scheme subset and how the 61A interpreter project evaluates it — parse, eval/apply, environments. Read the interpreters chapter of Composing Programs closely; then the ideas loop back to lecture 1. Abstraction, all the way down. This is also your bridge to CSE341 later in the path.
notes.focus: Write one Scheme function (factorial) by hand. Then read the interpreter chapter and find YOUR earlier Python concepts inside it: environments, frames, closures — the whole course in one program.
